description: Hi! I am a young space explorer who loves planets, rockets and learning about space. I enjoy playing games, solving puzzles and thinking of creative ideas. I am interested in science, technology and space missions. I want to create a fun Space Mission Design Game where players can plan their own missions and make exciting decisions
summary: Real space missions are won or lost on trade-offs: a bigger solar array adds mass, mass burns fuel, fuel costs money. Students rarely get to feel this. PARALLAX makes them live it. It is a browser game where players run a mission from contract to debrief, following NASA's own process. They pick one of eight missions, from an Earth-observation satellite to a Mars lander and a JWST-class telescope, write a concept of operations, then engineer the spacecraft across ten stations. One engineering model ties every choice to mass, power, heat, delta-v, data, cost and risk. Then the rocket launches on autopilot, drops its stages and releases the spacecraft, and the player takes over: they fly it through a debris field with their own hand, steering by moving their palm, opening it to raise a shield and making a fist to brake. Landers touch down by hand before a rover drives out for samples, while batteries drain at night and data waits for ground-station passes. The debrief shows what failed and why, beside the real NASA mission that did the same job. ATLAS, an AI mentor grounded in NASA material, coaches without ever taking over and can speak its alerts. Webcam gestures switch on only while flying and need no install. PARALLAX runs from a single HTML file on any school computer, for one to four players, turning mission design from a lecture into a decision you live with.
details:
1. The Problem

Every real spacecraft is a compromise. A bigger solar array adds mass; more mass needs more fuel; more fuel needs a bigger rocket and a bigger budget. NASA engineers spend their careers balancing these pulls. Yet space mission design is usually taught as a list of facts - a spacecraft needs power, a radio, fuel - so students never feel the trade-offs that decide whether a mission works. Tools that do model them are built for professionals, not for a 15-year-old with 40 minutes and a school laptop.

2. What PARALLAX Does

PARALLAX puts the player in charge of a NASA-style mission, from contract to debrief, on four numbered screens:

  1. Missions: choose one of eight mission contracts, read the briefing, write a concept of operations (ConOps) and pick a priority - Science first, Efficiency first or Lifetime first - which changes how the mission is scored.
  2. Build: engineer the spacecraft in an engineering cockpit with ten stations: Flight Plan, Instruments, Structure, Power, Propulsion, Thermal, Avionics, Comms, Ground and Launch (the telescope mission adds a Science Goal station). Each station has a status light and alerts, the spacecraft updates live in 3D, and gauges track mass, power, heat, delta-v, data, cost and risk.
  3. Launch & Fly: the rocket launches on autopilot in a short film, then the player flies the spacecraft through a 60-second debris field. Orbiters then manage power, data and emergencies month by month. Landers are steered down by hand, then a six-wheel rover drives across a cratered surface to collect samples.
  4. Debrief: see what worked, what failed and why, compare the design with the real NASA mission that did the same job, and act as the science team, choosing a conclusion the returned data actually supports.

Two more screens complete the experience: NASA Resources: linking every NASA source the game is built on, and ATLAS AI, the in-game mentor.

Figure 1. The game loop: four numbered screens that follow how NASA develops a real mission.

Eight missions, eight real NASA comparisons

Figure 2. Choosing a mission contract. Completing contracts earns XP and unlocks better parts.

Chart 1. PARALLAX engineering model, starter design for each mission. Simulation values; budgets in $ millions of game money.

All numbers the game produces are labelled as simulation values. Facts about real missions are sourced and linked, never invented.

3. How It Works – Key Innovations

One engineering model behind everything

A single function, calc(), turns any design into a full set of budgets: mass, power made versus power used, battery hours through darkness, temperature, delta-v left after arrival, data generated versus data sent home, cost, reliability and lifetime. A second function, risks(), reads those budgets and raises caution or NO-GO alerts, each with a plain-language fix, such as “Over budget: drop an expensive part, pick a cheaper rocket, or choose simpler instruments.” The same model drives the build gauges, the station lights, the flight and the final score. What a player learns while building is exactly what happens in flight.

Figure 3. calc() and risks(): one model feeds the gauges, the trade-offs, the flight, ATLAS and the score.

Figure 4. The engineering builder: stations with status lights on the left, the spacecraft in 3D in the centre, live gauges on top.

Trade-offs players can see and measure

Every part shows what it gives and what it costs. The Trade-offs tab plots every option for a station on one map and lists what each switch does to science, mass, power, cost, lifespan and data. Players are rewarded for balance, not for buying the most expensive part, and can save up to three alternative designs to compare, the way engineers do. The charts below are produced by the game's own model, and show the kind of trade-off players meet on their first Mars mission.

Figure 5. The Trade-offs tab: every power option on one map, with what each switch does to science, mass, power, cost, lifespan and data.

Chart 2. PARALLAX engineering model (calc()), Ares Surveyor starter design with each power option swapped in. Simulation values.

Chart 3. PARALLAX engineering model: delta-v from the same tank as spacecraft mass grows. Simulation values.

NASA's real process as the game's structure

Players move through NASA's Concept Maturity Levels: from an idea, to a concept of operations, to a design that passes review, to flight. A Mission Design Lab style equipment list shows every part with its margin. The ground segment (antennas and the flight team) is a station of its own, because data only comes home during ground-station passes.

Launch on autopilot, then fly the debris field yourself

The launch is a short film the player watches, not a test: the rocket lifts off past the tower, passes max-Q, drops its first stage, opens its nose cone above the atmosphere and releases the spacecraft. On rover missions the spacecraft is a cruise stage with the rover packed inside its aeroshell, the layout NASA used for Curiosity and Perseverance; orbiters unfold their solar wings.

Figure 6. The autopilot launch film, styled like a live launch webcast: speed and altitude gauges, an event timeline and captions from ignition to spacecraft separation.

Then the player takes the controls. For 60 seconds the spacecraft flies through rock and space junk that grows as it approaches, and more of it aims at the player as the round goes on. Anything on a collision course gets thin red brackets. The shield blocks hits but drains while held and has to recharge; the brake slows everything down but uses limited fuel. Hull left, dodges and hits become the flying score, which sets how much fuel the mission has for the rest of the flight, and a breached hull damages instruments.

Figure 7. The debris field on a Mars mission (cruise stage) and an Earth mission (satellite). The shield bubble, collision brackets, progress through the field and the systems panel are visible.

The debris field is designed so that one trick is not enough. When a test-pilot bot flew it with different strategies, only dodging and saving the shield for close calls survived the full round.

Chart 4. Debris Run engine (drcore.js), 12 automated runs per strategy by a test-pilot bot, 60-second round. Simulation values.

A flight that tests the design

Flight is a simulation driven by the design, not a scripted cut-scene. The battery drains at night, cameras need daylight, data waits for ground-station passes, radiation can upset the computer and fuel limits lifespan. Mission events - a solar storm warning, a degraded solar array, a ground station outage, a collision warning - pause the flight and hand the crew a decision. Missions to the Moon, Mars, the asteroid and Europa end with a hand-flown landing (touch down under 2.5 m/s inside the green circle; Mars adds a parachute), then a rover drive across a cratered surface with a live minimap to collect samples.

Figure 8. Entry, descent and landing: the player fires thrusters to touch down gently inside the green circle.

Figure 9. Surface operations: drive the rover across craters, collect samples and follow the live minimap.

Figure 10. Challenges and emergency commands appear during flight, with the controls at the side.

The proof is in the flight data. Because flight follows the engineering model, design choices show up as measurable results. Below, the same Earth-observation mission was flown twice by our automated tests. The under-powered version still finished its three years, but its battery ran low every month, instruments had to wait, and it scored 87 instead of 100.

Chart 5. PARALLAX flight simulator: Terra Watch flown twice by an automated test, starter design vs. the same design with body-mounted solar and a small battery. Simulation values.

ATLAS: an AI mentor that never takes over

ATLAS answers questions from a knowledge base of NASA material and explains why something failed. It can suggest a fix but never changes the design itself; the player stays the engineer. With the optional ATLAS server it uses a large language model (Gemini or Groq) with the API key kept on the server; without it, ATLAS falls back to a built-in rule-based advisor, so the game always works offline.

Built for every kind of player

At the start, players choose whether ATLAS should speak. With voice on, warnings, mission events and answers are read aloud using the browser's built-in speech, and the text always stays on screen.

Hand gestures are a flying tool, not a menu tool. When a player chooses Use gestures while flying, the webcam switches on only during a flight and off again afterwards, so menus and building stay simple with mouse, keyboard and touch. In flight, the hand becomes the controller: in the debris field the palm steers, an open palm raises the shield, a fist brakes and a thumbs-up starts; during the landing the hand steers the lander and a pinch fires the thrusters; on the surface the hand drives the rover with smooth, analog steering, a fist brakes and a pinch collects a sample. Hand tracking runs inside the browser tab: nothing to install, and the video never leaves the computer.

Figure 11. Before the game starts, players choose whether ATLAS speaks.

Figure 12. The start guide: hand gestures are only used while flying, and each flight stage shows what your hand does there.

A game, not a website

Every screen fits on one page with no scrolling, and a starter spacecraft with a guided tour lets a beginner fly first and then build their own.

Figure 13. The starter tour explains why each part of the ready-made spacecraft was chosen.

4. A Playthrough: One Choice, Many Consequences

Mission brief. The player takes the Mars contract (Ares Surveyor), writes a short concept of operations - map the surface from orbit, then land and collect samples - and picks Science first.

First build. They load extra instruments. The Power station turns red: power used is higher than power made, and the battery cannot carry the spacecraft through the night. ATLAS flags it, and with voice on it says so out loud. The Trade-offs tab shows the choices: bigger solar arrays cost mass and money; a radioisotope power source costs far more. The player chooses bigger arrays.

The ripple. The extra mass means the same tank now leaves less delta-v after arriving at Mars, so Propulsion turns amber. The player upgrades the engine, which pushes cost close to the budget, so they drop one lower-priority instrument. Every station is green and the design passes review.

Figure 14. The ripple from the Mars playthrough.

Flight. The rocket launches on autopilot and releases the cruise stage, with the rover packed inside its aeroshell. Then the player flies it through the debris field: their palm steers, and they open their hand to raise the shield only for close calls, because the shield drains. A clean run earns extra fuel. On the way to Mars, night passes test the battery and data only comes home during ground-station passes. Then the landing: the parachute opens, the player fires thrusters to touch down under 2.5 m/s inside the green circle, and drives the rover to collect samples using the minimap.

Debrief. The score breaks down science, tasks, resources, budget, communications, lifetime and flight operations, weighted by the chosen priority. The player sees why the mission went the way it did, compares the design with NASA's Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter, and analyses the data that reached Earth.

One small engineering choice rippled through power, mass, fuel, cost and science. That ripple is the lesson PARALLAX is built to teach - and no textbook can make a student feel it the way a battery running flat over Mars does.

5. Impact

Who it is for. Middle school, high school and early university students; teachers who want a ready-made engineering design activity; and anyone curious about how space missions are built. One to four players can share a computer and split real mission roles — Flight Director, Spacecraft Engineer, Science Officer, and Comms & Data — so it works as a team exercise.

What players learn.

  • Systems thinking: one change ripples through power, mass, fuel, cost and science.
  • How NASA develops missions: concept maturity, reviews, equipment lists with margins and ground operations.
  • Why real missions look the way they do, by comparing their own design with Landsat 9, SOHO, LRO, MRO, OSIRIS-REx, Europa Clipper, JWST and others.
  • How scientists work with limited data: the debrief asks players to choose a conclusion the data actually supports.

Why it works as a game. Players learn by failing safely. A mission that runs out of power at night teaches more than a paragraph about batteries. Eight missions, three telescope levels, three scoring priorities and a debris field that gets harder every second make it worth replaying.

Chart 6. PARALLAX scoring weights (PRIORITIES in the game code).

Access for everyone.

  • No install, no account and no server: one HTML file runs on school computers and older laptops (with a lower graphics setting).
  • Optional spoken alerts from ATLAS help players who prefer listening, or who are watching the spacecraft instead of reading.
  • Hand gestures switch on only while flying (debris field, landing, rover), so menus stay simple; keyboard, mouse and touch always work.
  • Plain-English text throughout, and every simulation number is labelled as one.

6. How PARALLAX Is Built

The game is built from a base file plus 21 extension modules, combined by a build script into a single parallax.html.

Figure 15. Architecture: everything runs in the browser; the Python helpers are optional.

The debris field is also packaged as Debris Run, a standalone single-file game: a 90-second round with a mirrored webcam preview showing the 21 tracked hand points, and a full keyboard fallback when there is no camera. Its code is commented so students can follow how hand landmarks become game controls.

Figure 16. Debris Run as a standalone game, with the shield on and the HUD showing hull, shield and brake fuel.

The models inside PARALLAX

Every mission is tested automatically

Automated browser tests fly every mission from launch to debrief, step the physics for landing and rover drives, fly the debris field with a test-pilot bot, and check that every screen fits without scrolling at 1280×720, 1366×768, 1440×900 and 1920×1080.

7. What's Next

  • Classroom mode: a teacher dashboard to assign missions, collect debrief scores and run class challenges.
  • More missions, each paired with its real NASA counterpart in the debrief.
  • More languages for the interface and ATLAS's voice.
  • Deeper trajectory planning, such as transfer windows, building on what GMAT models.
  • Online multiplayer, so a team can design one spacecraft from different computers.
  • Classroom playtests to measure learning with before-and-after quizzes.

Use of Artificial Intelligence (AI)

  • Claude (Anthropic) was used to help write and test the game's code (including the launch film and Debris Run), to build the pitch deck and to draft this write-up. The team designed the game, made the decisions and reviewed the results.
  • Inside the game, the optional ATLAS server sends player questions, together with passages from a NASA knowledge base, to a large language model (Google Gemini or Groq). Without the server, ATLAS uses a rule-based advisor and no AI service is called.
  • Gesture control uses Google's MediaPipe hand-tracking model, which runs on the player's own computer.
  • All images in this write-up are screenshots of PARALLAX, diagrams made for this write-up, or charts drawn from data exported from the game's own engineering model and flight simulator. No AI-generated pictures are used.
